segments.title: The modified Taiho as Japan's next fleet carrier
segments.body: The modified Taiho was a separate fleet-carrier project from the Unryu class, with five projected ships numbered 5021 through 5025. At roughly 38,500 tons full load and 33 knots, it belonged to the new generation of 35,000- to 45,000-ton ships expected to combine air power with substantial protection. The planned air group included 18 fighters and 27 strike aircraft, with additional aircraft also envisaged. Improved armament formed part of the design. In this comparison, a carrier of roughly 20,000 tons had shifted from the fleet standard of the 1920s and 1930s toward the upper end of the light-fleet category as designers moved beyond treaty ceilings.

evidence.note: Five projected modified Taihos, their separation from Unryu, and the stated displacement, speed, aircraft complement and fleet-carrier role.

segments.summary: Japan's modified Taiho project combined a 38,500-ton hull with greater protection, illustrating the growth of fleet carriers beyond treaty-era sizes.

segments.title: Treaty tonnage forced armor-versus-air-group choices
segments.body: Popular comparisons often say the United States chose air-group size while Britain chose armor, but all three leading carrier navies wanted both. A 27,000-ton design could combine the two, yet cumulative treaty allowances permitted only about five such ships for Britain or the United States and roughly three for Japan. Maintenance and refit would leave only two or three available in the larger fleets and perhaps one in Japan's. Cutting designs back toward 20,000 tons therefore imposed severe tradeoffs among protection, aircraft capacity, and the number of usable hulls.

evidence.note: The 27,000-ton design comparison and estimates of total and available carriers under cumulative treaty allowances.

segments.summary: British, American, and Japanese carrier designers wanted both protection and large air groups, but cumulative treaty limits made that combination too costly in hull numbers.

segments.title: Lift placement around the modified Taiho's armored box
segments.body: The angular lifts combined usable platform space with a shape intended to make alignment for a penetrating hit harder. A preference for simpler square lifts rests on ease of aircraft handling, accepting a compromise in that protective geometry. Placing lifts at the ends of the armored box limited openings in protected structure. An opening through the side could also interfere with anti-aircraft gun positions, a constraint shared with British armored-carrier designs. Later British proposals were already moving toward more numerous lifts. A further move away from centerline lifts is suggested as a possible development, rather than something that actually happened. Heavier armament and improved anti-torpedo protection formed part of Japan's intended second generation after Taiho.

evidence.note: The rationale for angular lifts, a preference for square platforms, and the protective and anti-aircraft constraints on lift placement.

segments.summary: The modified Taiho's unusual lifts illustrate the conflict between easy aircraft handling and preserving the integrity of an armored hangar box.

segments.title: Why Britain and Japan both needed survivable carriers
segments.body: British planners expected the major carrier war to occur in the Pacific while their heaviest repair infrastructure remained in the North Atlantic. A badly damaged ship might therefore have to survive a long voyage home before receiving full yard support. Japan's difficulty was its construction capacity, which could not match either the British Empire or the United States. These different constraints made damage tolerance and the preservation of every expensive carrier strategically important to both navies.

evidence.note: British Pacific war planning placed major repair work far from home yards, while Japan faced limits on replacement construction.

segments.summary: Different industrial constraints pushed both Britain and Japan toward carrier survivability: distant repair yards for one and limited replacement capacity for the other.

segments.title: The Royal Navy's unrealized 1931 carrier study
segments.body: The 1931 study preceded the design work that produced Ark Royal. A hypothetical schedule based on Ark Royal puts an order in 1932, laying down in 1933, launch in 1935 and commissioning in 1936. Accepting roughly 60 aircraft instead of 72 offered scope for better torpedo defense. Designers considered 4.5-inch and 4.7-inch dual-purpose weapons, with single and twin mountings among the options, so an earlier order could have advanced their development for wartime destroyers. A carrier entering service in 1936 would also have required earlier Fleet Air Arm expansion and might have brought forward the administrative settlement represented by the 1937 Inskip Award, which restored naval control of the Fleet Air Arm. Most later British carrier orders followed the removal of cumulative limits under the Second London Naval Treaty, reducing the need for this earlier hull to displace those programmes.

evidence.note: The 60-versus-72-aircraft tradeoff, earlier dual-purpose gun development and Fleet Air Arm expansion, and the end of cumulative limits before later carrier orders.
Alternative single and twin dual-purpose mountings and a hypothetical construction schedule based on Ark Royal.

segments.summary: An earlier British carrier could have accelerated dual-purpose gun work, Fleet Air Arm expansion and its return to Royal Navy control, and operational experience before Ark Royal.

segments.title: How British carrier studies turned missions into compromises
segments.body: British constructors began by defining the carrier's missions and sketching an ideal ship of roughly 27,000 tons. They then compared that ideal with the tonnage the navy was willing or permitted to allocate and removed capabilities until the design fitted. Cumulative treaty allowances therefore affected which parts of an otherwise desirable design survived into an order. Different priorities produced the 1931 studies' generous lifts and flagship accommodation, Ark Royal's emphasis on aircraft numbers and the Illustrious class's emphasis on survivability. The design papers preserve the reasoning behind compromises that are harder to explain by comparing completed ships alone.

evidence.note: An ideal 27,000-ton carrier reduced to an allocated tonnage, with contrasting aircraft-handling, flagship and protection priorities.

segments.summary: British constructors began with a mission-driven ideal carrier, then removed capabilities until it fit the tonnage the navy was willing or allowed to allocate.

segments.title: The 1931 carrier's larger lifts and flagship accommodation
segments.body: Some 1931 carrier studies allowed fighters to travel on one or two lifts with their wings spread. Ark Royal's later lifts required aircraft to fold their wings completely, so the earlier proposals offered a different approach to moving aircraft between hangar and flight deck. The 1931 designs also devoted more space to the bridge and flag accommodation. Contemporary jokes about designing the Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers' flagship connected that emphasis with Henderson, who then held the post. His later tenure as Third Sea Lord linked this earlier thinking with Ark Royal and the armoured-carrier programme, although those designs gave greater priority to aircraft capacity or survivability.

evidence.note: Wing-spread lift alternatives, larger bridges and flag spaces, and the connection with Henderson's carrier command and later design responsibilities.

segments.summary: Fighters with unfolded wings and more generous flag accommodation distinguish the 1931 studies from Ark Royal's later priorities.

segments.title: Deck parking could expand British carrier air groups
segments.body: The study's nominal 60-aircraft figure described hangar capacity rather than a hard operational ceiling. British experiments showed that the North Sea could be too rough for exposed aircraft, while the Mediterranean, Indian Ocean, much of the Pacific, and equatorial Atlantic offered more favorable conditions. Four to eight fighters could sit ready on deck, accompanied by a small number of patrol or anti-submarine aircraft for rapid response to a contact. Selective deck parking therefore increased both practical air-group strength and the speed of urgent launches.

evidence.note: Regional limits on deck parking and the example of four to eight ready fighters alongside a few patrol or anti-submarine aircraft.

segments.summary: The nominal 60-aircraft capacity of the 1931 study could grow through selective deck parking outside the roughest operating areas.

segments.title: An early carrier could have joined scattered British programs
segments.body: Building the 1931 carrier could have connected development programmes that struggled to secure funding and coordination separately. Britain had carrier tonnage available while capital-ship construction lacked a budget. An approved carrier project would have provided a common reason to advance the associated aviation, weapons and construction work. Experience from building it could then have fed into Ark Royal, followed by the Illustrious and Implacable classes. These are proposed consequences of an earlier order, judged with hindsight about the later programmes' needs.

evidence.note: The counterfactual links an earlier carrier order to coordinated funding, practical construction experience and later British designs.

segments.summary: Building the 1931 design might have connected underfunded aviation, weapons, and construction work while feeding experience into later carrier classes.

segments.title: French paper studies preserve interwar carrier thinking
segments.body: France built few interwar carriers but generated a large succession of studies and redrawn proposals. Navies that actually constructed ships often absorbed yard experience informally, so the paper record jumps between designs without preserving every reason for the change. French designers instead kept reacting on paper to domestic requirements and foreign developments. Their studies provide historians with an unusually continuous record for reconstructing how carrier ideas circulated and evolved across several navies.

evidence.note: French paper studies preserve successive responses to carrier ideas, while construction experience elsewhere can leave changes undocumented.

segments.summary: France's many unbuilt studies provide an unusually continuous paper trail for comparing how carrier ideas evolved across navies.

segments.title: A French hybrid carrier tried to fit colonial roles into 20,000 tons
segments.body: The proposal combined six 8-inch guns with upper and lower hangars and a split aviation arrangement. Torpedo aircraft would launch from lower-deck catapults near the heavy guns, while fighters would use the upper flight deck. The complexity reflected France's worldwide colonial and maritime obligations under a cumulative allowance of only 60,000 tons. That allowance left room for three 20,000-ton carriers rather than two 27,000-ton ships, but any design at the lower figure had to reconcile too many roles within one compact hull.

evidence.note: Six 8-inch guns, two hangar levels and split aircraft launches, set against colonial commitments and a 60,000-ton allowance.

segments.summary: An interwar French proposal combined heavy guns, split flight operations, and multiple hangars while trying to satisfy global commitments under a 60,000-ton allowance.

segments.title: Heavy guns tempt carriers into the wrong fight
segments.body: The objection to cruiser-caliber carrier guns concerns the decisions they encourage. Six- or 8-inch weapons may give a commander false confidence that the carrier can remain near a surface action instead of using speed and distance to preserve aviation power. The Royal Navy's wartime examples include losing one carrier in a surface engagement and another remaining in the firing line at Cape Matapan. In the Matapan account, the carrier fired its 4.5-inch guns while admirals urged it away from the fighting. The resulting design preference is to avoid armament that encourages a carrier commander to accept a cruiser-style gunfight.

evidence.note: The objection to heavy guns rests on encouraging risky surface action, with a British wartime loss and the Cape Matapan anecdote as examples.

segments.summary: Giving a carrier cruiser-caliber guns can encourage commanders to accept surface action instead of using speed and distance to preserve aviation power.

segments.title: U.S. baby carriers could extend cruiser scouting
segments.body: Several navies explored carriers below the Washington Treaty's 10,000-ton threshold. American studies alternated between a ship dedicated to scouting and fighter operations and a cruiser-carrier armed with 8-inch guns. The dedicated aviation role offered a way to extend reconnaissance across the Pacific, complementing the long-range coverage supplied by PBY Catalina flying boats. Assigning a small carrier to each cruiser squadron would give that formation its own reconnaissance and fighter cover. The accompanying cruisers would supply gun power and protect the carrier from opponents that closed the range. This division of work depended on keeping the flight deck focused on aviation rather than drawing it into the cruisers' surface fight.

evidence.note: American gun-armed and scouting-carrier alternatives, Pacific reconnaissance requirements, PBY coverage and the division of duties with cruiser squadrons.

segments.summary: Sub-10,000-ton U.S. studies make the most sense as specialized fighter and reconnaissance carriers supporting cruiser squadrons across the Pacific.

segments.title: Ryujo and Commandant Teste show different answers to limited tonnage
segments.body: The proposed route to a viable sub-10,000-ton carrier was to restrict its duties from the outset. Ryujo illustrates the criticism of trying to fit a full fleet carrier's responsibilities into that allowance. Some British and American paper designs receive a more favourable assessment because they demanded less of the hull. France took a different direction with Commandant Teste, emphasizing seaplane carriage, support operations and mobile naval basing. That choice made aviation support a purpose in its own right instead of requiring a small ship to duplicate every fleet-carrier function.

evidence.note: Restricted British and American design missions, criticism of Ryujo's fleet-carrier ambitions, and Commandant Teste's seaplane-support and mobile-basing role.

segments.summary: Small-carrier viability depended on the mission: Ryujo pursued fleet-carrier functions, while Commandant Teste concentrated on seaplane support and mobile basing.

segments.title: Hybrid warships can lose focus in both missions
segments.body: Combining two major roles in one hull looks economical in peacetime because a navy appears to buy broad coverage with fewer ships. In combat, however, a hybrid can meet an opponent optimized for either role and prove inferior in both. Compatible secondary functions such as point defense, naval gunfire support, or a backup anti-submarine capability can coexist, but the primary mission must still govern sensors, maneuvering, and command attention. An area-air-defense ship cannot let submarine hunting distract it from the air picture. A carrier exchanging gunfire likewise cannot coordinate reconnaissance effectively, potentially leaving the cruisers it supports surprised or outnumbered.

evidence.note: Peacetime savings from hybrid hulls, compatible secondary missions, and the loss of aircraft coordination when a carrier joins a gunfight.

segments.summary: Combining two major roles in one economical hull can leave it inferior to specialized opponents and distract its crew from the mission that matters most.

segments.title: Reference books for tracing carrier design
segments.body: The carrier references include Japanese Aircraft Carriers 1920-1945 and French Aircraft Carriers 1920-2000. Norman Friedman's U.S. Aircraft Carriers: An Illustrated Design History supplies another national design history, with ship plans by A. D. Baker III. British Carrier Aviation is valued for its hand-drawn archival design sketches. A newer British volume provides fold-out plans of Ark Royal, Victorious and Glorious across four A4 pages. The distinction between preliminary sketches and detailed ship plans gives readers different ways to examine proposals and completed designs.

evidence.note: Five carrier references, including named Japanese, French, American and British titles, with a comparison of archival sketches and fold-out plans.

segments.summary: A compact reading list points viewers toward illustrated design histories and plans for Japanese, French, American, and British carriers.

segments.title: PA9's specialized hangars left little room for aircraft growth
segments.body: PA9 was optimized for the aircraft doctrine and technology current when it was drawn. A forward fighter hangar had its own takeoff ramp over the bow, while two large lifts served the larger aircraft and their hangar spaces. The arrangement divided hangar capacity into three zones, including one restricted to fighters, and left the main flight deck short of the full hull length. Later growth in fighter, torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance-aircraft dimensions would have undermined those assumptions. Accommodating the wartime generation of aircraft would have required a full-length flight deck and extensive hangar reconstruction. Otherwise, space reserved for particular aircraft types could have become unusable even while the ship struggled to carry and sustain an adequate air group.

evidence.note: PA9's bow takeoff ramp, two large lifts and three specialized hangar zones, followed by a retrospective assessment of the rebuilding larger aircraft would require.

segments.summary: The French PA9 allocated space to specific aircraft types, creating a substantial rebuilding problem once larger wartime aircraft arrived.

segments.title: Design slack makes warships easier to modernize
segments.body: A design optimized around one precise forecast can become expensive to adapt when aircraft develop differently. One proposed improvement to PA9 is to provide three equally sized, flexible hangar spaces, each able to take any of the aircraft types. Assigning one to fighters would then be an operational choice that could change without reconstructing the ship. Large open hangars can look old-fashioned beside tightly specialized arrangements, yet Ark Royal's generous spaces underpin the retrospective argument that she would have been promising for postwar jet conversion had she survived. Spare capacity also matters across the fleet, where sufficient ship numbers leave room to adapt. Space and capacity retained at the design stage can reduce later alteration costs and extend useful service.

evidence.note: Three interchangeable hangar spaces as an alternative to PA9's specialization, the hypothetical Ark Royal jet conversion, and spare capacity in individual ships and the fleet.

segments.summary: Generous, flexible internal volume can outlast a tightly optimized layout when aircraft, technology, and missions change unexpectedly.

segments.title: Unryu and Ibuki reveal Japan's emergency carrier choices
segments.body: The Unryu programme accepted whatever engines, gearing and armor could be obtained to produce carriers with a useful air group quickly. This reliance on available equipment is the basis for classifying them here as light fleet carriers, distinct from the more ambitious modified Taiho. Ibuki offered an existing cruiser hull for conversion, although her 1943 launch never led to service as a carrier. An air-defense cruiser is raised as another possible use of the hull, with suitable armament identified as the obstacle. Conversion to a fast oiler was also considered as Japan faced an acute shortage of those ships. An extra flight deck would have been useful only if Japan could supply aircraft and trained aviators, and aircrew had become the more serious constraint.

evidence.note: Unryu's dependence on available machinery and armor, Ibuki's incomplete carrier conversion and alternative uses, and the shortage of trained aircrew.

segments.summary: Japan pursued adaptable carrier hulls from available machinery and cruiser construction, but ships alone could not replace lost aircraft and trained aircrew.

segments.title: Japan's attrition plan depended on the enemy cooperating
segments.body: Japanese planning envisioned a sequence of attritional attacks against an advancing fleet followed by a decisive battle near the home islands. The intended attrition phase would prepare that engagement without becoming a prolonged war of replacement. Japan's main fleet would remain fresh until the enemy had been reduced close enough to parity for the final battle. That concept depended on the opponent continuing a concentrated advance despite mounting losses, instead of withdrawing or choosing a different approach. Shortages of aircraft, trained aircrew and supplies then restricted attempts to adapt a force structure built around that sequence. Ibuki's conversion illustrates an effort to adapt, while the inability to provide crews strengthens the argument for preserving existing ships through better survivability.

evidence.note: A short attrition phase leading to battle with a fresh fleet, the assumption of a continuing enemy advance, and the crew and supply constraints on adaptation.

segments.summary: Japanese doctrine expected attritional attacks to weaken an advancing fleet before a decisive battle, but offered few alternatives when the enemy refused that script.

segments.title: Chatfield and Henderson reveal power inside naval administration
segments.body: Ernle Chatfield's authority as First Sea Lord encountered Reginald Henderson's influence as Third Sea Lord. The relationship is characterized as one in which Henderson would first humor a proposal, then try to dissuade Chatfield and, if necessary, expose its weaknesses. On that reading, Henderson's entrenched position made him difficult to remove or reposition before he wished to leave. Chatfield consequently faced limits on his ability to direct his own administration despite his formal seniority. Their disagreement places the small-carrier proposals within the practical distribution of power inside the Admiralty.

evidence.note: A characterization of Henderson's resistance to Chatfield's proposals and the administrative difficulty of removing or repositioning an entrenched subordinate.

segments.summary: The First Sea Lord's formal authority did not guarantee control when an entrenched Third Sea Lord possessed the design expertise and institutional position to resist him.

segments.title: Chatfield's treaty strategy favored many small carriers
segments.body: After the First World War, politicians sought to avoid another war, reduce weapons spending and support domestic reconstruction, with reelection also part of the calculation. Cumulative treaty limits forced navies to choose between numerous modest ships and fewer individually powerful ones. Chatfield's proposed solution sought international ceilings around 20,000 to 25,000 tons for capital ships and 17,000 to 22,000 tons for carriers, preferably lower still. Britain's larger allowance could then produce more hulls for worldwide duties. The strategy depended on other navies accepting those ceilings and on treaty diplomacy preventing the appearance of substantially larger competitors.

evidence.note: Post-First World War political motives for limits and Chatfield's proposed small-ship ceilings to maximize numbers within Britain's allowance.

segments.summary: First Sea Lord Ernle Chatfield sought international limits low enough for Britain to exploit its larger allowance through greater numbers of smaller capital ships and carriers.

segments.title: Large carriers concentrate more usable air power
segments.body: Carrier capability does not increase in a simple one-for-one relationship with displacement. For ships designed at the same time to the same standards, larger hulls can devote a smaller proportion of their space to machinery, leaving more room for aircraft and weapons. The comparison concerns the air group a ship can support and sustain in operations, including its sortie generation. In the illustrative 17,000-versus-27,000-ton matchup, several smaller carriers would have to be available in the same place to compete with the larger ship's usable air group. They would also have to coordinate multiple flight decks and commands against aircraft operating within a single organization. Displacement alone therefore gives an incomplete measure of the usable force a navy can assemble.

evidence.note: The machinery-space argument compares engineering-plant requirements as a proportion of larger hulls.
Same-period, same-standard design comparisons connect hull size with aircraft support, sortie generation and the difficulty of concentrating several small carriers.

segments.summary: Carrier capability does not rise linearly with displacement, and several small ships may struggle to coordinate the air group one larger carrier can operate together.

segments.title: Small carriers could support Britain's fleet carriers
segments.body: The useful version of the small-carrier concept adds aviation ships alongside fleet carriers rather than substituting them for the main striking force. Ordering smaller ships after the Second London Naval Treaty could have supported Britain's dispersed cruiser formations and worldwide commitments. One proposed alternative was to build four or five Unicorn-type forward aviation support ships in parallel with the Illustrious class. Replacing Ark Royal or the armored carriers with small decks, however, would sacrifice the concentrated air groups required for major fleet operations.

evidence.note: Small carriers alongside the main fleet and the proposed four or five Unicorn-type ships for dispersed cruiser and aviation-support duties.

segments.summary: Smaller carriers could support cruiser formations and global commitments, but replacing Ark Royal or the Illustrious class with them would sacrifice concentrated combat power.

segments.title: Treaties could not erase knowledge of larger warships
segments.body: An international agreement can restrict construction while established design ideas and technical knowledge remain available. A hypothetical ceiling of 20,000 tons and 12-inch guns would still leave larger ships such as Hood visible to rival navies. Colorado, Nelson and Rodney would likewise demonstrate that 16-inch guns remained possible. If strategic conditions deteriorated, existing designs and knowledge could support renewed construction of larger ships. The risk for a navy invested in small carriers or battleships is how quickly a competitor could produce those larger alternatives and outclass its force.

evidence.note: The limits of suppressing ideas and the hypothetical 20,000-ton, 12-inch ceiling, with existing large ships and 16-inch guns as counterexamples.

segments.summary: Low tonnage ceilings remained fragile because agreements could halt construction without making navies forget that larger carriers, battleships, and guns were possible.

segments.title: Ideological purity and the problem of political successors
segments.body: A criticism of communism here treats its repeated historical experiments as failures ending in brutal dictatorship, while the ideal continues to attract advocates. In this interpretation, demands for ideological purity allow ambitious people to pass loyalty tests and acquire power without demonstrating good conduct. Political systems that depend on unusually virtuous leaders remain vulnerable to ordinary human weaknesses. Even granting a founder's good intentions leaves the question of whether successors would behave as well. This political analogy introduces the related difficulty of suppressing a technological idea once people know it is possible.

evidence.note: A critical interpretation of communist experiments, ideological-purity tests and human fallibility, followed by the question of whether a founder's successors would govern well.

segments.summary: A political analogy links the persistence of communist ideals to ideological-purity tests, human fallibility and the uncertainty of succession.

segments.title: Counterfactuals test when paper carriers could matter
segments.body: The closing exercise assumes that a paper carrier reaches service and asks which later decisions or operations would change. Completed modified Taihos with trained air groups are judged too late to alter Japan's defeat, although fighter-heavy groups introduce the possibility of a stronger protective screen for Yamato's final sortie. The British 1931 alternatives raise a design choice: a full-length flight deck receives preference, while the larger lifts remain a point of interest. PA6 is the French proposal singled out for imagining the consequences of an earlier carrier in service. American sub-10,000-ton carriers introduce a diplomatic counterfactual: ships entering service before the London Naval Treaty could give the United States a reason to resist closing that loophole. These are possible consequences to examine, not outcomes established by the unbuilt designs.

evidence.note: Hypothetical modified-Taiho fighter cover for Yamato, a preference among 1931 British layouts, PA6 in service and American incentives to preserve the treaty loophole.

segments.summary: Imagine modified Taihos covering Yamato, an earlier British or PA6 carrier, or U.S. small carriers changing the incentive to close a treaty loophole.
